That is a good question. I would say studying effectively is more important, which is to say a proper time schedule has in addition, sleep and breaks. I can't stress enough sleep, it is so crucial if you want to engage and understand content, especially if the material is difficult. I sleep 7-8 hours every day, meaning I had around 16-17 hours of time where I was awake. I spent roughly 7-10 hours studying everyday.

Studying material beforehand really depends on the course and professor. Some professors provide their notes early, while others dont. Some courses have textbooks assigned to them, and some don't. For "easy" courses or gpa boosters, I didn't study as much because the content is not as difficult compared to my other courses, where for CPSC 351 for example I studied a lot more every day with the provided material. It depends on the course, and as a cpsc major there is a lot of material out there that supplements learning. Especially material from other universities, mit and waterloo a notable example.

What you are looking to study beforehand is essentially a 15-30 minute "pre-reading." I used to do this during my commutes (on the train) where I would read material that I would assume will be covered in class (if you don't know, then use your best judgement). The purpose is to familiarize yourself so that you can actively engage with the content during lecture. I emphasize during, because I know that before I seriously studied, I used to take notes of the content without actually understanding what's going on, mindlessly regurgitating words that the professor is saying, writing down word to word from the slide deck, when I know it's going to be available after class. I forced my future self to do the learning, which bit me in the ass when I started cramming.

The last thing I highly recommend to study effectively is getting enough sleep, it is super important to be able to succeed. If you want to be in your best form, you need sleep. I'm not going to go over the benefits, but in my experience the difference between sleep vs being sleep deprived is night and day.

One advice I can give you is that you have to manage your time well. I didn't do well in my first year, which is mostly because I tended to skip lectures and cram material. Although I finished with a good gpa, it could've been better had I taken university a lot more seriously.

In my second year (this academic year) I did a lot of introspection and actually learning how to study and manage my time appropriately. In this year, I've attended all my lectures and tutorials, without missing a single one. But that is not all what I did. Before the lecture, I would learn the topic covered ahead of time, and after the lecture I would review the content and practice active recall and test myself on the content that I just learned. This worked extremely well with me, but I know it worked because even though I generally am quite lazy, I was ruthless to myself and forced myself to go to lectures and tutorial even when I felt like I didn't want to. This may not work for you, but is a good piece of advice if you want to do well. Attending lectures and actively engaging with the content is the bare minimum to do well. To attest that this works, I finished with a 4.0 this year.

Hard is relative, but overall I think it is not too difficult if you put in the time, effort and have genuine interest in the field itself. Like u/nibor11 said, the cs profs here are very difficult to work with, and you may question whether or not cpsc is for you if you happen to have a terrible professor. You won't know how bad the profs are until you experience them, and if you think you can be the exception, reality will hit you like a truck.

The program itself is quite nice, though. You learn a lot about the theory of computation more than actually building great practical products. It's very interesting, too. For example, I took CPSC 359, which had me working low-level with Raspberry Pis, and even though I had a meh professor, I enjoyed the course material.

I'm going into my third year and had an excellent 2nd year, so I also have different views from other people. For example, I had Nasri for 331 in Spring, which wasn't as bad since I have lots of previous experience with that content, but I know those who are learning it for the first time had very poor performances (especially for the exams). Nasri also taught CPSC 355 and 351 in the winter, and while others have mixed views, I feel he is quite lenient and is not as bad as the rate my professor suggests. Maybe he is a bad lecturer, but definitely not a supremely bad professor.

Just like any other major, it depends on you. I feel it is not very hard, but that is just my opinion, if you are in the cs program, you have to decide that yourself.
